modelAnswer: The facial artery terminates by anastomosing with the dorsal nasal artery (a branch of the ophthalmic artery), forming rich collateral anastomoses at the angle of the mouth and near the nose. It also anastomoses with the transverse facial artery and the labial arteries.

The external arcuate fibers (cerebellar climbing fibers) arise from the olivary nuclei, particularly the inferior olivary nucleus. They pass through the hilum of the inferior olivary nucleus and cross the midline to reach the contralateral cerebellar cortex via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

The olivospinal tract (olivary tract) originates from the inferior olivary nucleus of the medulla oblongata. These fibers descend in the spinal cord within the lateral funiculus and terminate on interneurons in the intermediate gray matter, primarily at cervical levels.

The anterior spinal artery (ASA) supplies the medial medulla and the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. It arises from the vertebral arteries and descends through the anterior median fissure, supplying the pyramids, medial lemnisci, and corticospinal tracts.

The posterior spinal arteries (usually paired) supply the posterior one-third of the spinal cord. They arise from the vertebral or posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA) and run along the dorsal roots, supplying the dorsal columns and dorsal horns.

The three external features of the ventral (anterior) medulla are: (1) Pyramids — longitudinal ridges containing corticospinal fibers; (2) Olivary prominences — formed by the underlying inferior olivary nuclei; (3) Ventral lateral sulcus — between the pyramid and olive, from which the hypoglossal nerve emerges.

A cerebellopontine angle tumor (commonly vestibular schwannoma / acoustic neuroma) affects CN VIII (vestibulocochlear nerve) causing hearing loss and tinnitus; CN V (trigeminal nerve) causing facial numbness; and CN VII (facial nerve) causing facial palsy. Brainstem compression may also occur.

The three elevations of the closed medulla are: (1) Medial eminence (fasciculus gracilis) — medial, overlying the gracile nucleus; (2) Sulcomarginal area — lateral to the medial eminence; (3) Inferior olivary swelling — the prominent olive formed by the inferior olivary nucleus laterally.
General somatic efferent (GSE) cranial nerve nuclei include the oculomotor (CN III), trochlear (CN IV), abducent (CN VI), and hypoglossal (CN XII) nuclei supplying extraocular and tongue muscles.

The olfactory nerve (CN I) passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. The filaments of CN I traverse the foramina in the cribriform plate to reach the olfactory bulb. Fractures here can cause anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea.

The optic canal transmits the optic nerve (CN II) and the ophthalmic artery. The central retinal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery that enters the optic nerve. The ophthalmic artery is a branch of the internal carotid artery at the lateral aspect of the optic chiasma.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) runs in the interpeduncular fossa, in front of the tentorial edge (tentorium cerebelli crossing). It exits the brainstem between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries, entering the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus just below the trochlear nerve.

The trochlear nerve (CN IV) is the smallest cranial nerve and exits the brainstem at the dorsal surface of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus. It wraps around the cerebral peduncle and runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, anterior to CN III at the tentorial edge.

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) passes through the hypoglossal canal (anterior condylar canal) of the occipital bone. It exits the skull to supply the intrinsic and most extrinsic tongue muscles, mediating tongue movements and shape changes for speech and swallowing.

The inferior alveolar nerve (branch of V3) gives off: (1) Mylohyoid nerve — motor to mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric; (2) Dental branches — to mandibular teeth; (3) Incisive nerve — to mandibular premolars, canine, and incisors; (4) Mental nerve — exits mental foramen to chin and lower lip.

The pterygoid plexus drains into the retromandibular vein via the maxillary vein, which joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein. It also communicates with the facial vein via the deep facial vein and drains into the cavernous sinus via emissary veins.

The three contents of the carotid triangle are: (1) Common carotid artery (bifurcates into internal and external carotid at upper border of thyroid cartilage); (2) Internal jugular vein (lateral to artery); (3) Vagus nerve (posterior to artery, between IJV and ICA).

The contents of the muscular triangle include: (1) Sternothyroid and sternohyoid muscles (forming the floor); (2) Superior thyroid artery; (3) Superior laryngeal nerve and its branches (internal and external laryngeal nerves); (4) Lymph nodes and the thyroid gland.

The vagus nerve (CN X) gives off the following branches from the superior vagal (jugular) ganglion: (1) Meningeal branch — to the dura mater of posterior cranial fossa; (2) Auricular branch — to the external auditory meatus and a small area of the external ear. These are sensory branches.
Very light sleep (Stage N1) is characterized by theta wave EEG activity (4-8 Hz), vertex sharp waves, and loss of alpha rhythm, representing transition from wakefulness to sleep.

Tyrosine hydroxylase (or tyrosine 3-monooxygenase) is the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis. It converts tyrosine to L-DOPA, requiring tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) as a cofactor. This step is irreversible and tightly regulated by feedback inhibition.

Monoamine oxidase (MAO) is the primary enzyme catalyzing oxidative deamination of biogenic amines, including catecholamines and serotonin. It is located on the outer mitochondrial membrane and uses FAD as a cofactor. MAO inhibitors (MAOIs) are used as antidepressants.
Dopamine is primarily inactivated to homovanillic acid (HVA) via combined MAO and COMT activity; CSF HVA levels are used clinically to assess dopamine turnover.
Epinephrine and norepinephrine are metabolized primarily to vanillylmandelic acid (VMA) via combined MAO and COMT pathways; 24-hour urinary VMA is diagnostic for pheochromocytoma.

Parkinson's disease is the neurodegenerative movement disorder caused by progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency in the striatum.

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine) is synthesized in CNS neurons (raphe nuclei), enterochromaffin cells of GI tract, and platelets, where it acts as a neurotransmitter, hormone, and local signaling molecule.

Histamine and nitric oxide are the primary neurotransmitter vasodilators; histamine acts via H1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle while NO acts directly on vascular smooth muscle to cause relaxation.

Biogenic amine neurotransmitters include: (1) Catecholamines: dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), and epinephrine (adrenaline); (2) Indolamine: serotonin (5-HT); (3) Imidazoleamine: histamine. They are synthesized from aromatic amino acids and act on G-protein coupled receptors.

Acetylcholine (ACh) effects include: (1) Muscarinic effects: decreased heart rate, increased GI motility and secretions, bronchoconstriction, pupil constriction (via M2/M3 receptors); (2) Nicotinic effects: skeletal muscle contraction, ganglionic transmission (via nAChR). ACh is inactivated by acetylcholinesterase.
The principal end product of catecholamine synthesis in the urine is vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), formed by the combined actions of MAO and COMT on epinephrine and norepinephrine metabolites.

GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is derived from glutamate (glutamic acid) via decarboxylation by glutamate decarboxylase (GAD), requiring pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor. GABA is the principal inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.

Based on function, neurotransmitters are classified as excitatory (causing depolarization/action potentials), inhibitory (causing hyperpolarization), or modulatory (altering neuronal sensitivity without direct excitation/inhibition).

Glutamate is the principal excitatory neurotransmitter in the CNS. It acts on NMDA, AMPA, and kainate receptors, mediating fast synaptic transmission, plasticity, and excitotoxicity. It is cleared by astrocytic uptake and converted to glutamine.

The substrates for glutamate transaminase (GOT / aspartate aminotransferase) are glutamate and oxoglutarate (alpha-ketoglutarate), yielding aspartate and glutamate as products. It requires pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) as a cofactor and plays a key role in transamination reactions.

The main pathway of deamination for amino acids is oxidative deamination, catalyzed by L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). GDH converts glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and NH3, using NAD+ or NADP+ as coenzymes. The released NH3 enters the urea cycle for excretion.

The product of transdeamination of glutamine is glutamate. Glutaminase deamidates glutamine to glutamate and NH3 in the mitochondria. Glutamate then undergoes oxidative deamination by GDH, completing transdeamination and releasing ammonia for the urea cycle.

NAD+ (or NADP+) is the coenzyme required for L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH). GDH catalyzes the oxidative deamination of glutamate to alpha-ketoglutarate and NH3, using NAD+ as cofactor. This reaction is reversible and occurs in the mitochondria.

L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is stimulated by GDP, ADP, and other purine nucleotides (positive allosteric effect), which increase its affinity for glutamate. These activators promote oxidative deamination, particularly during fasting when ammonia disposal is needed.

L-glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is inhibited by GTP, ATP, and high concentrations of glucocorticoids. These negative allosteric regulators suppress GDH activity to conserve glutamate for other metabolic processes and prevent excessive ammonia production.

D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO) is found in the liver, kidneys, and brain (cerebellum). It catalyzes the oxidative deamination of D-amino acids to their corresponding keto acids, producing H2O2 and NH3. Deficiency is linked to schizophrenia.

Ketoglutarate-D-amino acid oxidase (DAAO) flavoprotein acts on neutral D-amino acids such as D-serine, D-alanine, and D-proline. It uses FAD as a prosthetic group and produces alpha-keto acids, H2O2, and NH3.

Alanine aminotransferase (ALT / alanine transaminase) converts pyruvate to alanine in muscles. This reaction transfers the amino group from glutamate to pyruvate, forming alanine and alpha-ketoglutarate. Alanine is then transported to the liver for gluconeogenesis.

Ammonia (NH3) released by deamidases in the liver enters the urea cycle. It is first converted to carbamoyl phosphate by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the mitochondria, then combines with ornithine to form citrulline, ultimately leading to urea synthesis for excretion.

NH3 released by deamidases in the kidney is excreted in urine as NH4+ (ammonium ion). Renal ammoniagenesis involves deamination of glutamine by glutaminase and glutamate dehydrogenase, producing NH3 which diffuses into the tubular lumen and binds H+ to form NH4+ for excretion.
The major mechanism of ammonia excretion in the liver is urea synthesis via the urea cycle, which converts two molecules of ammonia (one free, one from aspartate) into one urea molecule.

The first step of the urea cycle is the formation of carbamoyl phosphate from NH3 and CO2, catalyzed by carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) in the mitochondrial matrix. This step consumes 2 molecules of ATP and requires N-acetylglutamate (NAG) as an obligatory activator.
Ornithine transcarbamoylase catalyzes the second step of the urea cycle, transferring the carbamoyl group from carbamoyl phosphate to ornithine, forming citrulline.

The second step of the urea cycle is the synthesis of citrulline from carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine, catalyzed by ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC). Citrulline is then transported to the cytosol for the remaining steps.

The final step of the urea cycle is the hydrolysis of argininosuccinate to form arginine and fumarate, catalyzed by argininosuccinate lyase. Arginine is then cleaved by arginase to produce urea and ornithine, completing the cycle.

The mitochondrial enzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis is carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II), distinct from the cytosolic enzyme; the question may refer to amidophosphoribosyltransferase or dihydroorotate dehydrogenase.
The urea cycle consumes 3 ATP molecules (equivalent to 4 high-energy phosphate bonds): 2 ATP for CPS I reaction and 1 ATP for argininosuccinate synthetase (AMP + PPi effectively = 2 ATP).

The main fate of urea is excretion in urine. Urea is filtered by the glomerulus and partially reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. About 60-70% of filtered urea is excreted daily, with plasma concentration maintained at 2.5-7.5 mmol/L.

N-acetylglutamate (NAG) is the obligatory activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I). NAG is synthesized from acetyl-CoA and glutamate by N-acetylglutamate synthase (NAGS), and its synthesis is stimulated by arginine, the product of the urea cycle.

The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. It arises from C1-C5 spinal segments, ascends through the foramen magnum, joins the cranial part, and exits via the jugular foramen to innervate these muscles for head rotation and shoulder elevation.

The arteries supplying the pons include: (1) Basilar artery (main supply) — gives off pontine arteries; (2) Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) — from basilar, supplies lateral pons and middle cerebellar peduncle; (3) Superior cerebellar artery (SCA) — from basilar, supplies the upper pons.

The venous drainage of the thalamus is via the thalamostriate veins, which drain into the internal cerebral veins. These veins ultimately drain into the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and then into the straight sinus. The thalamus also drains via the basal vein to the great cerebral vein.

The neostriatum (striatum) consists of the putamen and caudate nucleus, separated by the internal capsule. It is the major input structure of the basal ganglia, receiving cortical, dopaminergic (from substantia nigra pars compacta), and thalamic inputs. It projects GABAergic neurons to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.

The venous drainage of the basal ganglia is via the striate veins (thalamostriate veins), which drain into the internal cerebral veins and then the great cerebral vein (of Galen). These veins ultimately drain into the straight sinus. The basal ganglia also drain via the basal vein to the great cerebral vein.

The basal ganglia are involved in: (1) Motor control — planning, initiation, and regulation of movement (via direct and indirect pathways); (2) Cognition — working memory and executive functions (prefrontal connections); (3) Emotion and motivation (limbic connections via nucleus accumbens). Dysfunction leads to Parkinson's disease (hypokinetic) or Huntington's disease (hyperkinetic).

Spasticity is a velocity-dependent increase in tonic stretch reflexes (hyperreflexia) with hypertonia, resulting from UMN lesions above the spinal level. Rigidity is a constant, uniform resistance throughout the range of motion (lead-pipe or cogwheel) due to basal ganglia disorders. Spasticity involves exaggerated tendon jerks; rigidity involves normal tendon jerks.

The posterior spinal arteries (PSAs) arise from the vertebral arteries or the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries (PICA), usually as paired vessels. They descend along the dorsal roots, supplying the posterior columns and posterior horns of the spinal cord, receiving reinforcement from radicular arteries.

L-DOPA (L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) is the immediate metabolic precursor of dopamine. It is formed from tyrosine by tyrosine hydroxylase (the rate-limiting step) and is converted to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) in the cytosol.

Carbidopa (or benserazide) is the peripheral inhibitor of DOPA-decarboxylase (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase) used in Parkinson's disease treatment. It prevents peripheral conversion of L-DOPA to dopamine, reducing side effects and increasing CNS availability of L-DOPA.

Alpha-methyl tyrosine inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine synthesis, blocking conversion of tyrosine to DOPA and reducing catecholamine production in pheochromocytoma.

Yes, histamine is a vasodilator, particularly in postcapillary venules. It also increases vascular permeability, stimulates gastric acid secretion (via H2 receptors), and acts as a neurotransmitter in the CNS (H3 autoreceptor). Histamine acts via H1, H2, H3, and H4 receptors.

Neomycin, an aminoglycoside antibiotic, is used in hepatic coma to reduce ammonia-producing gut bacteria. It acts by inhibiting protein synthesis in intestinal bacteria, decreasing ammonia production from amino acid deamination and urea hydrolysis by bacterial urease.
